labs.title: Buffer Manager and 2Q Replacement
labs.subtitle: Turn page requests into safe, concurrent access to a bounded in-memory buffer while preserving dirty data.
assignment_brief: Implement a buffer manager for configurable page and buffer sizes. A 64-bit page identifier uses its high 16 bits as the segment id and its low 48 bits as the page number inside that segment; each segment is persisted in a file named by the segment id.

fix_page(page_id, exclusive) must return a resident frame protected in shared or exclusive mode, loading the page on a miss. unfix_page(frame, dirty) releases the caller's fix and records modifications. When no free frame remains, a 2Q-style FIFO/LRU policy must choose an unfixed victim or throw buffer_full_error.

The concurrency requirement is part of the algorithm, not an optional optimization: unrelated page requests must continue while one thread waits for a page latch, and the global manager latch must not cover slow disk I/O.
learning_outcomes: Trace a buffer hit, buffer miss, dirty eviction, and buffer-full failure while preserving the page-table and pin-count invariants.
Simulate the assignment's two-list replacement policy and explain why one-time scan pages stay separate from pages that demonstrate reuse.
Explain the different jobs of the page table, buffer frame, pin count, dirty flag, replacement metadata, page latch, manager mutex, and per-segment file latch.
Write deadlock-aware fix/unfix pseudocode that releases the global manager mutex before ordinary page-latch waits and disk I/O.
Separate buffer-manager durability from transaction recovery: writing dirty pages is necessary, but WAL/LSNs are outside this exercise.

concepts.title: Resident pages, frames, and the page table
concepts.takeaway: A page is a persistent logical block; a frame is one reusable memory slot that currently contains some page.
explanation: The manager preallocates page_count frames, each with page_size bytes. page_table maps a full 64-bit page id to the frame that currently contains it, so a buffer hit is expected O(1). Frame identity is stable, but its page_id and bytes change after eviction; callers must not retain or use get_data() after the final unfix.

The page id is split as [16-bit segment id | 48-bit segment-local page id]. The segment selects a file; the local page id multiplied by page_size gives the byte offset. A page beyond the current file end is returned as an all-zero page.
pseudocode: if file_size < offset + page_size: return zero_page
else: read page_size bytes at offset
invariants: Every resident page has exactly one page-table entry.
Every resident frame is in exactly one replacement queue: FIFO or LRU.
A frame with fix_count > 0 cannot be selected as a victim.
The frame's bytes are valid for the advertised page_id before another thread can acquire its page latch.
pitfalls: Confusing a page id with a frame number.
Using a frame's data after unfix, when the frame may already have been reused.
Forgetting that offset multiplication can overflow for hostile page_size/page_id inputs; this student implementation performs no explicit overflow check.

source_refs.note: Defines 2Q, 64-bit page ids, segment layout, configurable sizes, and concurrent fix/unfix.
Declares frame state, page table, queues, segment files, API, and page-id split helpers.
Preallocates frame storage and implements segment-offset reads with zero-fill beyond EOF.

concepts.title: The assignment's FIFO/LRU form of 2Q
concepts.takeaway: Give new pages one FIFO chance; only pages requested again earn space in the recency-managed hot queue.
explanation: A miss inserts the page at the FIFO tail. A hit on a FIFO page promotes it to the LRU tail; a hit on an LRU page refreshes it to the tail. Victim selection scans from the FIFO head for the first unfixed frame, then from the LRU head.

This resists scan pollution: pages touched once remain eviction candidates, while a reused index root reaches the hot queue. For exam answers, call this the course/assignment variant of 2Q. Canonical published 2Q is often described with queue-size targets and an A1out ghost-history queue, neither of which exists here.
pseudocode: on HIT(frame in FIFO): FIFO.erase(frame); LRU.push_back(frame)
on HIT(frame in LRU): move frame to LRU.back
victim := first frame in FIFO with fix_count = 0
if none: victim := first frame in LRU with fix_count = 0
invariants: Newly loaded pages enter FIFO.
A resident page's second request promotes it from FIFO to LRU.
The front of each queue is the first eviction candidate within that queue.
Fixed frames stay in their queue but are skipped during victim selection.
pitfalls: Calling this a complete implementation of every canonical 2Q variant; it has no ghost queue or explicit queue-size partition.
Evicting the queue head without checking fix_count.
Updating queue metadata without the manager mutex.
Assuming promotion occurs on unfix: this implementation updates recency when fix_page observes the hit.

source_refs.note: Implements queue transitions and FIFO-first victim search.
Promotes hits and inserts newly loaded frames into FIFO.
Specifies FIFO eviction, second-access promotion, and LRU refresh order.

concepts.title: Fix, latch, dirty, and unfix
concepts.takeaway: Pinning prevents replacement; latching controls concurrent byte access; dirty state decides whether replacement needs a write.
explanation: fix_count is the replacement pin count. page_mutex is the data-access latch: shared fixes may coexist, while an exclusive fix excludes all other access. dirty is sticky until a successful write path resets or removes the frame, so any unfix marked dirty makes later eviction/destruction write the page.

The interface does not pass the original lock mode to unfix_page. This solution therefore stores, per thread and per frame, the mode and recursive fix count. That supports repeated same-mode fixes without recursively locking std::shared_mutex. It does not correctly upgrade a nested shared fix to exclusive; the implementation returns early without checking the new exclusive request.
pseudocode: FIX(page, mode): increment global fix_count before waiting for page latch
if this thread already fixed frame: increment local nesting count; return
acquire frame latch in requested mode
UNFIX(frame, dirty): frame.dirty := frame.dirty OR dirty
if local_count > 1: decrement local_count and fix_count
else: unlock in remembered mode; erase local record; decrement fix_count
invariants: fix_count counts all outstanding fixes, including nested fixes.
A thread unlocks in the same shared/exclusive mode it originally acquired.
Dirty state is monotonic between load and write-back.
The last local unfix releases the page latch and one unit of fix_count.
pitfalls: Treating pinning and latching as the same mechanism.
Forgetting to mark a modified page dirty.
Attempting a shared-to-exclusive nested upgrade: the current code silently keeps only the shared latch.
Returning from a thread without balancing every fix; neither the latch nor fix_count is repaired automatically.
Calling unfix_page from a different thread: the thread-local record is absent and this implementation silently returns.

source_refs.note: Shows distinct dirty, fix-count, and page-latch state plus the public lifecycle contract.
Tracks lock mode and nesting per thread; the early return at 243-245 exposes the unsupported upgrade case.
Pinned frames cannot be evicted, and exclusive page access serializes concurrent increments.

concepts.title: Miss handling and dirty eviction
concepts.takeaway: Reserve and protect a frame under metadata synchronization, then perform slow write/read work after releasing the global manager mutex.
explanation: On a miss, the manager chooses an unused frame or an unfixed victim. It exclusively latches that frame, remembers a dirty victim's old page id, removes the old mapping, installs the new page's metadata and FIFO entry, and increments fix_count—all while holding manager_mutex.

After manager_mutex is released, a dirty old page is written, the requested page is read, and the exclusive frame latch is retained or converted to shared for the caller. Publishing the page-table entry before I/O is safe because other fixers increment the pin and then block on the frame latch; they cannot observe half-loaded bytes.
pseudocode: if unused frame exists: frame := unused frame
else: frame := FIFO/LRU victim with fix_count = 0; lock frame exclusively
remember old {page_id, dirty}; erase old page-table and queue entries
install new {page_id, fix_count = 1, dirty = false}; FIFO.push(frame); page_table[new] := frame
if old dirty: write old bytes to old page id
return with exclusive latch, or convert to shared
invariants: The dirty old bytes are written using the old page id before the frame data is overwritten.
No caller can observe a partly loaded page.
The global manager mutex is not held during disk I/O.
A miss-in-progress is pinned and therefore cannot itself become a victim.
pitfalls: Overwriting the victim before writing its dirty bytes.
Holding manager_mutex during disk I/O and serializing unrelated requests.
Publishing an unlatched, half-loaded frame.
Ignoring I/O exceptions: this solution uses raw latch lock/unlock and publishes new metadata before I/O, so a thrown open/read/write error can leave the frame latched and the mapping inconsistent.

source_refs.note: Complete hit/miss path, victim reservation, dirty write-back, read, and latch handoff.
Requires deadlock resistance and short global latch hold times around millisecond-scale I/O.
Checks persistence and that waiting on one page does not block unrelated page operations.

concepts.title: Segment files and resize coordination
concepts.takeaway: Cache one File object per segment and synchronize its cached size so block I/O remains race-free.
explanation: README warns that separate File objects referring to the same file are unsafe. segment_files therefore caches one SegmentFile per 16-bit segment id. A short file_mutex protects only lookup/creation of this map.

Each SegmentFile has a cached size and shared_mutex. Reads and in-range writes hold a shared lock, which allows the File API's thread-safe pread/pwrite calls to overlap. Extending the file uses an exclusive lock and a second size check. The global manager mutex is never needed for this work.
pseudocode: if sf.size >= required_size: write block; return
if sf.size < required_size: resize; sf.size := required_size
unlock exclusive; shared_lock sf; write block
invariants: At most one cached File object represents a segment within the manager.
The cached size is read or changed under that segment's mutex.
Resize is exclusive; block reads/writes may proceed concurrently once the size is sufficient.
Different segment files need not share one long-lived I/O latch.
pitfalls: Opening a new File object on every page request.
Checking size concurrently with resize without synchronization.
Claiming that the implementation holds no latch during I/O: it intentionally holds the frame latch and a per-segment shared latch, while avoiding the global manager latch.

source_refs.note: States that only block reads/writes are thread-safe and duplicate File objects are unsafe.

trace.title: A scan page loses to a reused page, and a dirty victim is written
trace.setup: Use three frames. All pages are initially absent. Show queues from oldest to newest and assume every fix is followed by unfix.
steps: Fix 1: miss; load it and place it in FIFO. State: FIFO [1], LRU [].
Fix 2: miss. State: FIFO [1, 2], LRU [].
Fix 1 again: hit; promote it to the LRU tail. State: FIFO [2], LRU [1].
Fix 3 exclusively, modify it, and unfix dirty. State: FIFO [2, 3], LRU [1]; page 3 is dirty.
Fix 4: the pool is full. Victim search starts at FIFO and evicts clean page 2. State after load: FIFO [3, 4], LRU [1].

Fix 5: FIFO is preferred again, so dirty page 3 is selected. While its frame is exclusively latched, write page 3 to its segment file, then read page 5 into the same frame. Final state: FIFO [4, 5], LRU [1].
trace.result: The once-touched pages churn through FIFO, the reused page 1 remains protected in LRU, and dirty data is persisted before frame reuse.

drills.prompt: Write fix_page miss-path pseudocode that is safe under concurrent requests for the same missing page.
drills.answer: Under the manager mutex choose and exclusively latch an unused/unpinned frame, remove the old mapping, install the requested page's mapping with fix_count 1 and FIFO membership, then release the manager mutex. Write the dirty victim if needed and read the new page while retaining the frame latch. A second requester may find the published mapping and increment fix_count, but must block on that latch until loading completes.
checklist: Never choose a fixed victim.
Remember the old page id before overwriting metadata.
Publish one page-table entry and one queue membership.
Release manager_mutex before disk I/O.
Use the frame latch to hide partial loading.

drills.prompt: Simulate FIFO and LRU after the reference string 1, 2, 1, 3, 4 with three frames under this assignment's policy.
drills.answer: After 1: FIFO [1], LRU []. After 2: FIFO [1,2]. The second 1 promotes it: FIFO [2], LRU [1]. After 3: FIFO [2,3], LRU [1]. Request 4 evicts FIFO head 2, so FIFO [3,4], LRU [1].

A hit on FIFO promotes to LRU.

drills.prompt: Why are fix_count and page_mutex both necessary?
drills.answer: fix_count protects residency: replacement skips any frame an operator is using. page_mutex protects the bytes: many readers may share it, but a writer needs exclusive access. A page can be unfixed yet remain resident, and a fixed page still needs a latch mode, so neither mechanism substitutes for the other.
checklist: Pinning versus mutual exclusion.
Replacement versus data races.
Shared reader and exclusive writer behavior.

drills.prompt: Debug this sequence in the submitted implementation: one thread calls fix_page(P, false), then fix_page(P, true) before either unfix.
drills.answer: The second call finds the frame in the thread-local map, increments only the local nesting count, and returns without upgrading the shared latch. The caller therefore does not receive the requested exclusive protection. A correct design must reject upgrades, provide an explicit safe upgrade protocol, or define that nested fixes must use a compatible mode.
checklist: Locate the early return at src/buffer_manager.cc:241-245.
State that fix_count still increments.
Explain why shared-to-exclusive cannot be silently treated as shared.
Propose a defined API behavior.

drills.prompt: Compare this implementation with canonical 2Q descriptions.
drills.answer: Both separate first-touch pages from reused hot pages. This assignment uses a resident FIFO plus resident LRU and always searches FIFO first. Canonical 2Q is commonly described with capacity tuning and an A1out ghost queue that remembers recently evicted first-touch pages. Do not invent that ghost queue when tracing the submitted code, and do not generalize the code as the only form of 2Q.
checklist: Resident FIFO for first touches.
Resident LRU for proven reuse.
No ghost history here.
Answer according to the variant named in the question.

drills.prompt: Does flushing every dirty victim make this buffer manager transactionally crash-safe?
drills.answer: No. Dirty write-back preserves page bytes across replacement, but a transactional DBMS must also enforce write-ahead logging, track page/log sequence information, and support undo/redo according to its steal/force policy. This exercise's BufferFrame has no page LSN and implements no log protocol.

limitations: README and tests define the assignment contract. The implementation is student work and the report is a later retrospective; neither should be presented as course ground truth.
The implementation is the assignment's simplified resident FIFO/LRU form of 2Q, not every canonical 2Q variant; it has no A1out ghost queue or explicit queue-size target.
Nested same-thread shared-to-exclusive fix upgrades are not supported correctly, and the public contract does not document that limitation.

labs.title: Slotted Pages, Stable TIDs, and Free-Space Inventory
labs.subtitle: Learn how a database turns one fixed-size page into movable records with stable logical addresses, then finds reusable space without inspecting every page.
assignment_brief: Implement the record-access layer beneath the provided database interface: a SlottedPage for variable-size records, an SPSegment for allocate/read/write/resize/erase, and a Free-Space Inventory that locates reusable pages through the BufferManager.

A table owns one slotted-page segment and one FSI segment. TIDs combine a segment-local page number with a stable slot number. If a growing record no longer fits on its original page, the original slot becomes a forwarding entry; repeated moves must rewrite that original forwarding entry instead of creating a chain.

The FSI must use compact approximate entries, live in buffer-manager pages, and span more than one page. The README explicitly warns that the supplied tests cover only obvious bugs, so page accounting, redirect ownership, FSI false positives/negatives, and buffer interactions need independent reasoning.
learning_outcomes: Draw the page header, upward-growing slot array, downward-growing record area, contiguous gap, and fragmented holes.
Maintain stable live-record TIDs while compaction changes physical record offsets.
Distinguish total reclaimable free space from immediately contiguous free space and decide when compaction is necessary.
Decode the project's tagged 64-bit slot as empty, local record, redirect, or redirect target.
Write one-hop resize/redirect pseudocode that preserves payload and reclaims the old target.
Explain conservative 4-bit FSI encoding, multi-page addressing, and the difference between buffer-resident visibility and actual disk persistence.
Connect the implementation to exam-style page drawings and hexdump decoding while recognizing the scan/recovery features this project omits.

concepts.title: Slots separate logical identity from physical byte position
concepts.takeaway: A TID names (page, slot); the slot names the current byte range, so compacting records changes offsets without changing live-record TIDs.
explanation: The page begins with a 12-byte header. Fixed-size eight-byte slots grow toward higher addresses immediately after it, while record bytes are allocated backward from the end of the page. The page is physically full when the slot frontier and record frontier meet.

TID stores a 48-bit segment-local page number above a 16-bit slot ID. get_page_id reattaches the segment ID in the upper 16 bits expected by BufferManager. Within a live record's lifetime, slot IDs are never renumbered by compaction.

Stable means stable across byte movement and redirection, not immortal. Erasing a record makes its slot reusable, so an old stale TID can later alias a different record; this format has no generation counter.
invariants: A live local slot's offset and length identify bytes within the same page.
A real zero-length record has length zero but a nonzero offset; only the reserved empty encoding is reusable.
Compaction may rewrite slot offsets but never changes the slot index of a live record.
slot_count covers every slot position up to the highest non-trimmed slot, including reusable holes.
first_free_slot is the lowest empty slot or slot_count when the slot array must grow.
pitfalls: Moving slot entries during compaction breaks every external TID.
Treating length zero alone as empty loses valid zero-length records.
Calling an erased TID permanently stable ignores slot reuse and the ABA/alias problem.
The project header omits the recovery LSN shown in the lecture, so this is a simplified physical format.

source_refs.note: Packs a segment-local page and 16-bit slot, then reconstructs a segment-qualified buffer page ID.

concepts.title: Total free space and contiguous free space are different state
concepts.takeaway: Deletes and moves create holes; the page counts them as reclaimable but delays record movement until a request cannot fit in the current gap.
explanation: header.free_space means the bytes that would be usable after compaction, including holes. The immediately usable gap is data_start minus the end of the current slot array. Their difference is fragmented free space.

Allocation first charges data bytes and, only when no reusable slot exists, one Slot. If total free space is insufficient it fails. If total space is sufficient but the current gap is too small, it compacts and retries.

Compaction visits only local data slots, orders them from high to low current offsets, memmoves live payloads against the end of the page, and updates each slot offset. Redirect and empty slots carry no local payload and are skipped.
pseudocode: for live local slots ordered by offset descending:
move payload against page end and rewrite slot.offset
invariants: free_space is never less than the current contiguous gap.
A middle erase adds payload length to total free space without moving unrelated live records.
A trailing empty slot can shrink slot_count and return its eight bytes to free_space.
After compaction, all reclaimable space is one contiguous gap.
Compaction preserves every live payload and the redirect-target flag stored in its slot.
pitfalls: Using total free_space as a memcpy destination bound without compaction can overwrite a live record.
Compacting eagerly on every erase adds unnecessary write amplification.
Copying records in an unsafe order can overwrite a payload that has not been moved yet.
data_start can remain below the true packed boundary after erasing several records; it is a conservative frontier until compaction, not proof that bytes below it are live.

source_refs.note: Defines the current slot frontier, data gap, and reusable-slot search.
Separates total from contiguous capacity and compacts only when required.
Creates holes for middle records, trims trailing empty slots, and preserves stable remaining slot IDs.
Moves live payloads safely and rebuilds offsets/frontiers.

concepts.title: Growing a record preserves its slot before it preserves its page
concepts.takeaway: Relocate first tries the same page; if that page cannot absorb the growth, SPSegment preserves the original TID with a one-hop redirect.
explanation: SlottedPage::relocate handles same-page changes. Shrinking keeps the offset and releases the length difference. Growing copies the old prefix, obtains a new local byte range, zero-fills the extension, and preserves the redirect-target marker.

If the original page lacks the additional total space, SPSegment allocates a target record elsewhere, copies min(old,new) payload bytes, marks the target, and replaces the original slot with the target TID. Point reads and writes follow at most one forwarding slot.

If an already redirected record moves again, the implementation resizes the existing target when possible. Otherwise it allocates a new target, rewrites the original redirect directly to it, and erases the old target. This prevents original→old→new chains and releases the abandoned space.
pseudocode: if source is local and relocate_in_page succeeds: return
invariants: The caller's original TID remains the point-access identity across every supported resize.
A normal resize copies the common prefix and zero-initializes newly added bytes.
A forwarding source contains no local payload; its old payload space is returned to its source page.
The original slot points directly to the current target, so supported API operations traverse at most one redirect.
Replacing a target erases the old target and updates both affected FSI entries.
pitfalls: Redirecting an already redirected target instead of rewriting the original source creates an unbounded chain.
Erasing only the source redirect leaks the target record and its FSI capacity.
Updating the source before the new target is initialized exposes incomplete data; this code initializes first, but the multi-page sequence still has no crash recovery.
Calling resize directly on a hidden redirect-target TID can create behavior outside the one-hop public-original-TID assumption; the target marker is not used to forbid it.

source_refs.note: Handles shrink/grow, overlap-safe payload copying, optional compaction, zero-fill, and marker preservation.
Checks additional capacity, updates FSI, frees the source payload, and installs a redirect.
Visits at most two slots: original plus one target.
Rewrites an existing redirect to a replacement target and then reclaims the old target.
Erases a redirect target before erasing the stable source slot.

concepts.title: The eight-byte slot is a tagged union
concepts.takeaway: The same 64 bits mean either (offset,length,flags) or a forwarding TID; the top-byte tag decides which interpretation is valid.
explanation: For a local slot, bits 0..23 hold size, bits 24..47 hold offset, bits 48..55 hold the redirect-target marker, and bits 56..63 are 0xFF. A local empty slot has offset=0, size=0, and that 0xFF local tag.

For a redirect, the entire 64-bit word is a raw TID and the top byte must not be 0xFF. A redirect target remains a local slot, but its marker byte is nonzero so a future scanner could distinguish relocated physical records.

The encoding makes a forwarding entry fit in the slot even when the page data area is completely full. That is the core lecture motivation: recovery or update can preserve the stable logical TID without finding extra bytes in the original page.
invariants: A slot must be interpreted only after checking its tag.
A redirect stores a same-segment target TID and no local offset/length.
A redirect target is still a local data slot and participates in compaction.
The target marker survives same-page relocation and compaction.
The 24-bit offset and size fields constrain the representable page/record range.
pitfalls: Reading redirect bits as an offset and size yields meaningless page addresses.
The top-byte tag reserves some TID patterns: set_redirect_tid rejects a TID whose top byte is 0xFF.
The implementation marks the target but does not store the original TID in the relocated payload, so it cannot implement the lecture's stable-identity scan rule by itself.
No sequential-scan API uses is_redirect_target; do not infer complete scan behavior merely from the marker.

source_refs.note: Defines tag tests, empty encoding, 24-bit offset/size fields, raw-TID redirects, and target marking.
Interprets tagged slots and toggles the physical-target marker.
Treats marked targets as local data and preserves their marker while changing offsets.
Exercises repeated point access through redirects but not scan-time original-TID reconstruction.

concepts.title: The FSI is a conservative, page-resident approximation
concepts.takeaway: Two four-bit entries fit in each byte; decoded capacity never exceeds actual capacity, so a match is safe, but coarse buckets can miss pages that really fit.
explanation: encode_free_space selects the largest code whose decoded lower bound is not greater than the measured free bytes. Therefore decode(encode(x)) <= x. This prevents an FSI code from promising more space than a page had when updated.

Each 1024-byte FSI page holds 2048 nibbles and therefore describes 2048 slotted pages. target page 2050 maps to FSI page 1, entry 2. update fixes that raw FSI page exclusively and changes only the selected half-byte.

find converts a requested size to the first code whose decoded lower bound can satisfy it, scans from a process-local rotating cursor, and wraps once. Comparing codes is valid because the decode table is monotone.

Conservatism has a cost. On a 1 KiB page, codes jump from 896 to max-free 1012. A page with 1000 actual free bytes encodes as 896, so find(900) rejects it. On 4 KiB pages, all non-completely-empty capacities above 896 collapse to the same code 14, making the FSI particularly incomplete for large records.
pseudocode: return largest code c with decode(c) <= actual_free
minimum = first code c with decode(c) >= required
scan encoded entries from rotating cursor, wrapping once
return first page with code >= minimum
invariants: One target page consumes exactly one four-bit FSI entry.
Updating one nibble preserves the other nibble in the byte.
decode(encode(actual_free)) never exceeds actual_free.
FSI page and nibble arithmetic works across page boundaries.
A returned page is still rechecked against exact current page state before allocation.
pitfalls: Conservative encoding prevents false promises but does not prevent false negatives.
Calling the FSI exact is wrong; its purpose is a compact candidate filter.
The hard-coded byte thresholds do not scale with page size except for code 15.
The rotating cursor is a process-global unordered_map keyed only by segment ID; it is neither persisted nor synchronized.
The supplied persistence test shares one BufferManager and therefore proves buffer-page residency, not survival across a database restart.

source_refs.note: Stores the process-local cursor, packs two entries per byte, and converts a byte request to a minimum code.
Implements conservative lower-bound encoding with fixed thresholds and a page-size-dependent code 15.
Maps a target page to an FSI page/nibble and writes it through BufferManager.
Scans multi-page nibbles from a rotating start position and wraps once.
Checks conservative decoding, basic lookup, and visibility through a fresh FSISegment sharing the same BufferManager.
Covers a threshold boundary and target page 2050 beyond the first 2048-entry FSI page.

concepts.title: SPSegment turns approximate hints into verified allocations
concepts.takeaway: It tries a locality hint, then the FSI, then creates a page; every candidate is checked using the real page header before bytes are reserved.
explanation: Allocation first rejects records larger than one page can hold. A process-global per-segment hint remembers the last successful page and is checked before an FSI scan, which helps append-like workloads with similarly sized tuples.

On a candidate page, the exact requirement depends on whether an empty slot can be reused. The candidate is fixed exclusively, its actual free-space state is checked, SlottedPage::allocate runs, and the new exact free-space value is written back to FSI.
If no existing page is used, table.allocated_pages is incremented, the schema is written, a fresh SlottedPage is placement-constructed in the next segment page, and both FSI and hint are updated.
pseudocode: if allocation_hint is valid and exact_page_check(hint, size): use hint
if candidate and exact_page_check(candidate, size): use candidate
invariants: No allocated record exceeds one page's header-plus-one-slot capacity.
An approximate FSI or stale hint is never trusted without an exact page check.
Every successful allocate, resize, redirect-source change, and erase updates the affected FSI entry.
table.allocated_pages defines the valid slotted-page scan/search range and is serialized in the schema.
A newly allocated record receives a segment-local page plus stable slot TID.
pitfalls: The FSI request always includes a new-slot charge, so it can miss a page that could reuse an empty slot; the exact hint path is less pessimistic.
If the single FSI candidate fails exact validation, allocation immediately creates a page instead of asking FSI for another candidate.
Schema page-count metadata is persisted before page construction succeeds, so exception/crash rollback is not demonstrated.
The global hint arrays are keyed only by 16-bit segment ID and are not thread-safe or scoped to a BufferManager/database instance.

source_refs.note: Defines process-global locality hints and the one-page record limit.
Implements hint, FSI, exact validation, new-page construction, schema write, and FSI refresh.
Associates SP/FSI segment IDs and the allocated slotted-page count with each table.
Serializes table.allocated_pages with the rest of the schema through buffer-manager pages.
Exercises allocation, random erase, larger allocation, and resize, but contains no correctness assertions.

trace.title: Delete a middle record, then compact only when a larger insert needs the hole
trace.setup: Use a 1024-byte page with a 12-byte header and eight-byte slots. Allocate A=200 bytes in slot 0, then B=200 bytes in slot 1. This extends the exam's insert-A/insert-B/delete-A drawing with one allocation that forces the implementation to use the reclaimed hole.
steps: After A: slot 0 points to offset 824, data_start=824, slot_count=1, and free_space=804.
After B: slot 1 points to offset 624, data_start=624, slot_count=2, and free_space=596.

Delete A. Slot 0 becomes the first reusable slot. B remains at offset 624 because deletion is lazy. Total free_space rises to 796, but the contiguous gap is still 624-(12+2·8)=596; the 200-byte difference is fragmentation.
Request C=700 bytes. Slot 0 can be reused, so only 700 bytes are required. Total free space is sufficient but the 596-byte contiguous gap is not, which triggers compactify.
Compaction moves B from offset 624 to offset 824 and updates slot 1. B's TID (page,1) and payload remain unchanged; all 796 reusable bytes become contiguous.
C is allocated into reused slot 0 at offset 124. data_start=124 and free_space=96.
trace.result: The final page contains C in slot 0 and B in slot 1. B moved physically but retained its logical TID. This trace demonstrates delayed compaction, stable slots, total-versus-contiguous free space, reusable slot overhead, and payload-preserving movement.

decisions.title: Stable slot numbers; movable payload bytes
decisions.rationale: Indexes and callers keep compact (page,slot) identifiers while the page is free to defragment record bytes and update only local offsets.
decisions.tradeoff: Every record pays eight bytes for indirection, and erased slot reuse means stale TIDs are not protected by a generation number.

source_refs.note: Defines the external page-and-slot identity.
Moves payloads and updates offsets without reordering slots.

decisions.title: Lazy compaction with a total-space counter
decisions.rationale: Deletes and shrinks are cheap; records move only when a request can fit after defragmentation but not in the current gap.
decisions.tradeoff: The header and allocation logic must track two notions of free space, and later allocation may incur an expensive full-page move.

source_refs.note: Compares total and contiguous capacity before deciding to compact.

decisions.title: Forwarding metadata lives in the slot
decisions.rationale: The original page can always hold a redirect after a growing update, even if another transaction has consumed all released data bytes.
decisions.tradeoff: The tag restricts representable bit patterns, and complete scan identity would require storing/deriving the original TID at the target—missing here.

source_refs.note: Multiplexes local record metadata and a raw TID in one fixed-size entry.

decisions.title: Rewrite the original redirect instead of chaining targets
decisions.rationale: Point access remains bounded to original plus one target, and replacing a target has predictable cleanup.
decisions.tradeoff: Resize becomes a multi-page copy/update/erase sequence with no demonstrated crash atomicity or concurrent protocol.

decisions.title: Four-bit conservative FSI entries
decisions.rationale: A tiny summary can reject obviously full pages without fetching each data page, and lower-bound decoding avoids unsafe overestimation.
decisions.tradeoff: The fixed bucket table creates safe but sometimes severe false negatives, especially for requests above 896 bytes and page sizes above 1 KiB.

source_refs.note: Selects the largest decoded lower bound not exceeding actual free bytes.

decisions.title: Process-local allocation and scan hints
decisions.rationale: The last successful data page and next FSI scan position avoid repeatedly searching from the beginning in append-heavy workloads.
decisions.tradeoff: Both hints are global, unpersisted, keyed only by segment ID, and unsynchronized; they are performance shortcuts, not durable metadata.

drills.prompt: Insert 200-byte A, insert 200-byte B, then delete A on a 1024-byte page. Draw slots, data_start, total free space, contiguous free space, and fragmentation.
drills.answer: Header is 12 bytes and each slot is 8. A is slot 0 at offset 824; B is slot 1 at offset 624. After deleting A, slot 0 is empty/reusable, slot 1 still points to B at 624, slot_count remains 2, first_free_slot=0, data_start=624, total free_space=796, contiguous space=596, and fragmentation=200. No eager compaction is needed.
checklist: Slots and records grow from opposite ends.
Keeps B at its old offset after lazy delete.
Marks slot 0 reusable without renumbering slot 1.
Separates 796 total from 596 contiguous bytes.
Identifies the 200-byte hole.

drills.prompt: Write compactification pseudocode that preserves TIDs and cannot overwrite an unmoved record.
drills.answer: Collect live local slot IDs, sort them by current offset descending, set next=page_size, and for each slot decrement next by its length, memmove the payload to next, and write only that slot's offset. Then set data_start=next and free_space=data_start-slot_end. Slot indices never move; redirects and empty slots are skipped.
checklist: Operates on slot IDs, not copied slot order.
Uses a safe movement order and memmove.
Updates every moved offset.
Does not move redirect entries as payload.
Recomputes frontiers from live state.

drills.prompt: Decode a 64-bit slot whose top byte is 0xFF, target byte is 0x00, offset is 0x000320, and size is 0x000040.
drills.answer: Top byte 0xFF makes it a local slot, target byte zero means it is not marked as a redirect target, offset 0x320=800, and size 0x40=64. Because offset and size are not both zero, it is a live 64-byte local record at page bytes [800,864).
checklist: Checks the tag before reading fields.
Converts offset and size correctly.
Distinguishes target marker from redirect tag.
Does not call a zero-size or nonzero-offset record empty.

drills.prompt: Give the one-hop algorithm for resizing a TID that already redirects when its target cannot grow in place.
drills.answer: Read the prefix from the old target, allocate and initialize a new target, mark it as relocated, rewrite the original source slot directly to the new target, then erase the old target and refresh both FSI entries. Never turn old_target into a redirect.
checklist: Starts from the original source and old target.
Copies min(old_size,new_size) bytes.
Initializes the new target before publishing it.
Rewrites the original redirect directly.
Erases the old target and updates FSI.

drills.prompt: Explain why decode(encode(x)) <= x is safe but insufficient to prove that FSI.find will find every page that fits.
drills.answer: The inequality means an entry never promises more free bytes than were measured, so a matching lower-bound code is safe. But rounding down loses information. With this table, 1000 free bytes on a 1 KiB page encodes to 896; a 900-byte request needs code 15 and rejects that page. Exact page validation protects against false positives, while false negatives only waste capacity.
checklist: Defines conservative lower-bound encoding.
Separates safety from completeness.
Provides the 1000→896 / request-900 example.
Mentions exact candidate recheck.
Identifies wasted space/new-page cost.

drills.prompt: Audit this claim: 'FSIPersistence proves free-space entries survive a database restart.'
drills.answer: The claim is too strong. The test destroys and recreates FSISegment but keeps the same BufferManager, whose in-memory page map retains the nibble. The supplied BufferManager explicitly performs no disk I/O and ignores dirty flags. The design routes FSI through normal pages, but restart persistence requires a real buffer/file manager test.
checklist: Identifies the shared BufferManager lifetime.
Notes dummy BufferManager has no disk I/O.
Distinguishes object state from page state.
States what an actual restart test would recreate.

drills.prompt: Compare the project's redirect target with the full lecture scan contract.
drills.answer: The project marks a target slot and point operations follow the original slot to it, preserving the caller's TID. The lecture additionally requires a sequential scan to ignore forwarding stubs and, on encountering the physical target, return the original stable TID. This code stores no original TID with the target payload and exposes no scan API, so the marker alone is insufficient for that behavior.
checklist: Credits one-hop point access.
Explains forwarding stubs are skipped during scans.
Requires original logical identity at the target.
Identifies the missing original-TID payload/scan API.
Does not generalize tests beyond what they cover.

lecture_links.note: Pages live in frames with shared/exclusive latches and dirty state; this is the storage contract SPSegment and FSI are written against, although the supplied test double omits those behaviors.
Why a compact FSI exists, how four-bit approximate classes trade precision for size, why linear scanning needs hints, and how locality knowledge can improve allocation.
Stable (page,slot) TIDs, opposing page growth, delayed compaction, header fields, reusable-slot hints, and the free-slot versus zero-length-record distinction.
The undo/update problem that motivates slot-resident redirects, tagged eight-byte slots, redirect-target marking, and the original-TID requirement for sequential scans.
Scope boundary: this project rejects any one record larger than a slotted page; true long records need BLOB/CLOB representations spanning extents or tree-like structures.

limitations: The student report is treated as commentary, not authority. Its claims were retained only where README, current source, tests, and independent traces agree.

The supplied BufferManager explicitly has no disk I/O, locking, eviction, page-count enforcement, or dirty handling. Segment and FSI code exercise the intended fix/unfix interface, but persistence, concurrency, and replacement behavior are not demonstrated.
FSIPersistence recreates only FSISegment while sharing one in-memory BufferManager. It proves page-backed rather than object-backed state, not survival across a new manager/process or disk restart.
The FSI's fixed thresholds top out at 896 before the special exactly-max bucket. This is conservative but can miss large usable gaps; the loss becomes extreme on 4 KiB pages used by the benchmark.

The lecture's page header includes an LSN for recovery; this project's 12-byte header does not. Redirect replacement and schema/page allocation are multi-page sequences with no WAL, crash atomicity, or rollback protocol.

The project marks redirect targets but stores no original TID with their payload and has no sequential scan API. It therefore does not implement the lecture rule that scans skip redirect stubs yet report a relocated record under its original logical TID.

TID/slot encodings use 24-bit size/offset fields and reserve a top-byte pattern to distinguish redirects. The implementation asserts against one class of raw TIDs but does not provide comprehensive page-size/page-number range guards.

Process-global FSI cursors and allocation hints are keyed only by segment ID, are not synchronized, are not reset per BufferManager/database, and are not persisted. They must be viewed solely as best-effort single-process shortcuts.

The full project test suite was not runnable because this checkout has no build directory and CMake is unavailable. Independent clang++ smoke programs did execute successfully for compaction/payload preservation, conservative and multi-page FSI behavior, one-hop redirect replacement, old-target reclamation, and erase.

Visible tests do not cover stale-TID slot reuse, direct operations on a redirect-target TID, cross-segment redirects, real table scans, crash points during redirect replacement, concurrent allocations/resizes, or actual disk reopen.

labs.title: Page-Resident B+-Tree
labs.subtitle: Turn page bytes, separator rules, and split propagation into an index you can trace and explain under exam pressure.
assignment_brief: Implement a templated B+-tree whose nodes live inside fixed-size buffer-manager pages and whose child references are page IDs rather than process pointers. The required public operations are insert, lookup, and erase; the assignment explicitly permits omitting links between leaf pages.

The concrete tests instantiate 64-bit keys and values, std::less ordering, and 1024-byte pages. They treat a repeated key as an update, force both leaf and multi-level splits, and require thread-safe behavior under four concurrent writers.

The README also asks for the concurrency techniques from the lecture's Concurrent Access (2) and (3) slides. The submitted implementation does not implement those techniques: it serializes every public operation with one tree-wide mutex. That distinction is essential for learning and for the recalled lock-coupling exam task.
learning_outcomes: Derive the physical capacity of leaf and inner nodes from page size, alignment, and entry width.
State one separator convention precisely and use it consistently for lookup, split, and parent insertion.
Write point-lookup and recursive split-propagation pseudocode without relying on C++ details.
Trace a full-leaf insertion through split, separator propagation, and root creation.
Distinguish the assignment's simple leaf erase from complete B+-tree deletion with redistribution and merge.
Explain why the tree-wide mutex is safe but not the lock-coupling, safe-page, or restart strategy taught in the lecture.

include/moderndbs/segment.h — segment identity and buffer-manager ownership
include/moderndbs/buffer_manager.h and src/buffer_manager.cc — in-memory fake page/latch environment

concepts.title: A node is a typed view over one database page
concepts.takeaway: The index is page-resident: a node is constructed in frame bytes, and durable-style page IDs—not C++ pointers—connect the tree.
explanation: Every page begins with a small Node header containing level and count. Level zero identifies a leaf. Leaf count means records; inner count means children, so an inner node with c children has only c-1 valid separators.

The template parameter PageSize allows capacities to be computed at compile time after aligning the data area. With the tested 1024-byte page and 64-bit key/value/page-ID fields, both capacities are 63 entries or children and each node occupies 1016 bytes.
The constructor allocates the first segment page, fixes it exclusively, and placement-constructs an empty LeafNode. New page IDs combine the 16-bit segment ID with a 48-bit segment-local page number.
invariants: Every LeafNode and InnerNode fits completely inside PageSize bytes.
level == 0 means leaf; a split preserves the level of the split node.
Leaf count is the number of aligned key/value pairs.
Inner count is the number of children; exactly count-1 separator keys are meaningful.
A child reference is a page ID in the B-tree's segment, never an in-memory node pointer.
pitfalls: Using inner count as the number of keys causes an off-by-one child access.
Ignoring alignment can make the arrays misaligned or push the object past the end of the page.
The implementation's next_segment_page and root are in-memory fields; it does not demonstrate restart-time metadata persistence.
The header depends on transitive includes for vector, optional, and mutex, which is brittle even though this project builds in its original environment.

source_refs.note: Defines the common header, aligned layout, inner capacity, separator array, and child page IDs.
Computes leaf capacity and lays out parallel key/value arrays.
Checks page fit and constructs the initial root leaf inside a fixed frame.
Builds segment-qualified page IDs and advances the local allocator.
Requires computed nodes to nearly fill, but never exceed, both 1 KiB and 64 KiB pages.

concepts.title: One separator convention controls every descent
concepts.takeaway: This implementation stores separator[i] = maximum key in child[i], so equality must descend left.
explanation: Both leaf and inner search use comparator-based lower_bound: the first stored key that is not less than the target. Equality is detected with !(a<b) and !(b<a), so KeyT need not implement operator==.

For an inner node, lower_bound searches only count-1 separators and its returned position is directly the child index. If the target exceeds every separator, the returned index is count-1, the rightmost child.
This max-of-left convention differs from the common min-of-right diagrams. Either convention can work, but lookup, split return values, and parent insertion must agree exactly.
pseudocode: lo = first i in [0, inner.count-1) with inner.keys[i] >= key
return lo                 // equality stays in child[lo]
return page.values[i] if exact match else NOT_FOUND
invariants: Leaf keys are strictly sorted because a repeated key overwrites its value.
For every non-rightmost child i, keys[i] is an upper bound and initially the exact maximum of children[i].
A key equal to keys[i] is routed to children[i], not children[i+1].
All tree operations call the same child-selection helper, avoiding divergent routing rules.
pitfalls: Returning the first key of the right page while retaining equality-goes-left lookup misroutes the boundary key.
Searching inner.count separators reads one unused array slot; the valid key count is inner.count-1.
Using operator== directly breaks the generic comparator contract.
Deletion may leave a stale but still safe upper bound in the parent; calling it the exact child maximum after arbitrary erases would be inaccurate.

source_refs.note: Binary-searches count-1 separators and returns the routing index.
Binary-searches records and detects equality only through ComparatorT.
Traverses page IDs and applies lower_bound in the final leaf.
Centralizes equality-left comparison and child selection.
The report correctly identifies max-of-left; this claim agrees with lookup and split code.

concepts.title: Insertion propagates a small split result upward
concepts.takeaway: A recursive call returns only separator, right-page ID, and level; the parent either absorbs that result or splits and forwards a new one.
explanation: At a leaf, an existing key is updated. A non-full leaf shifts larger records right and inserts in sorted order. A full leaf is split first; the new key is then inserted into the left or right half according to the returned max-of-left separator.

At an inner node, recursion follows one child. No returned result means no structural change. Otherwise the parent inserts the child's separator and right-page pointer. If the parent is full, it too splits and sends a SplitResult upward.
If the old root splits, public insert allocates a fresh inner root with exactly two children. This is the only height-increasing operation, preserving equal leaf depth.
pseudocode: if key exists: update value; return NO_SPLIT
if page has room: sorted_insert(page, key, value); return NO_SPLIT
sorted_insert(key <= sep ? page : right, key, value)
if s is NO_SPLIT: return NO_SPLIT
if page has room: insert_separator(page, s); return NO_SPLIT
if insert_recursive(root, key, value) returns s:
invariants: Duplicate insert updates exactly one existing value and does not increase leaf count.
Leaf split preserves sorted key/value pairing and returns max(left).
Inner insertion shifts keys and children in lockstep while the old left child stays at key_index.
A propagated split adds one child and one separator to its parent.
Root split creates a new level but never changes the levels of existing pages.
pitfalls: Overwriting children[key_index] instead of inserting the new right child at children[key_index+1] disconnects the old left half.
Creating a new root without retaining old_root as child zero loses half the tree.
Forgetting the duplicate-key update can create equal separators and violate the intended unique-key behavior.
The code holds exclusive page latches along the entire recursive path; its safety currently also relies on the outer tree mutex.

source_refs.note: Shifts a new right-child reference into the parent and divides a full inner node.
Implements update-or-sorted-insert semantics.
Copies the right half and returns the maximum key retained by the left leaf.
Consumes a root split by constructing a new two-child root.
Implements update, leaf split, parent absorption, inner split, and upward propagation.

concepts.title: The submitted erase is lookup-correct, not a full B+-tree delete
concepts.takeaway: It removes a record from its leaf but deliberately omits redistribution, merge, parent repair, root shrink, and page release.
explanation: Leaf erase lower-bounds the key, does nothing if absent, shifts later key/value pairs left, and decrements count. Tree erase descends with the same separator routing as lookup.

This is enough for the visible Erase test: every removed key becomes unfindable. Stale parent separators remain safe upper bounds, so point lookup still reaches the only page where the key could reside.

It does not preserve the lecture's non-root minimum-occupancy invariant. A complete deletion must borrow from a sibling with the same parent or merge, remove/update the parent separator, repair parent underflow recursively, and possibly shrink the root.
pseudocode: sibling = adjacent child of the same parent
if sibling can lend: redistribute and repair separator; stop
else: merge nodes, remove parent entry, continue at parent
if root has one child: make that child the new root
invariants: After the submitted erase, remaining records in the leaf stay sorted and key/value positions stay aligned.
Erasing an absent key is idempotent.
Point lookup remains correct even if an ancestor separator is a stale upper bound.
The minimum half-full occupancy invariant is not maintained by this implementation.
pitfalls: Presenting this method as complete B+-tree deletion would contradict both the lecture and the report's own limitation.
Marking the leaf dirty even when the key was absent is harmless in the fake manager but needlessly signals a write in a real system.

concepts.title: Safety today comes from serialization, not lecture lock coupling
concepts.takeaway: The tree-wide mutex prevents races, but it bypasses the concurrency algorithm that is both assigned and independently recalled as exam material.
explanation: lookup, insert, and erase each acquire the same std::mutex for their entire execution. Therefore no two public operations overlap; even read-only lookups are serialized. Lecture lock coupling instead latches parent, identifies the child, latches the child, and only then releases the parent. The root-to-leaf acquisition order avoids deadlock during ordinary descent. Insert is harder because a split propagates upward; acquiring an ancestor while holding a descendant reverses the order.

The lecture's safe-page strategy splits a full inner page while its parent is still latched, bounding later propagation. For variable-length keys, the restart strategy releases latches and retries with a deliberately protected full path. The current code's global mutex, not its page-latch protocol, is what serializes root changes and split propagation.

concepts.title: The iterator contract and stable output registers
concepts.takeaway: Control moves downward through next calls, but tuple values move upward through stable Register locations.
explanation: open prepares an operator and its children, get_output exposes the addresses of its current tuple registers, repeated next calls mutate those values, and close releases state.

Projection can expose a subset of child pointers, while a blocking operator must own one fixed-size output buffer. Reallocating that buffer during next would invalidate pointers already cached by the parent.
pseudocode: next(): advance child or local state; overwrite *out; return success
invariants: A successful next leaves every exposed output Register valid for the current tuple.
The addresses returned after open remain stable until close.
A false next means the stream is exhausted, not merely that one input tuple was rejected.
pitfalls: Returning pointers into a vector that grows during next.
Copying full tuples through every pass-through operator.
Forgetting to open or close children in the same lifecycle.

concepts.title: Streaming operators and pipeline breakers
concepts.takeaway: Classify the concrete algorithm, not just the operator name.
explanation: Select and Projection pass child tuples through immediately. Sort must consume the complete input before it can know the first result. HashAggregation must finish group state before final output.

HashJoin must finish its build side before probing, but a general implementation can stream probe matches. This submission additionally materializes all joined results. UNION ALL streams; UNION DISTINCT needs a growing seen set but need not inherently wait for both inputs.

one-sided breaker: build entire left; then probe right
full breaker: consume all required input; then next() scans materialized results
invariants: A pipeline begins only after the state required by its upstream breaker exists.
The label reflects when the first output can appear and which inputs must be consumed.

concepts.title: Set semantics versus bag multiplicities
concepts.takeaway: The ALL keyword changes the answer from membership to arithmetic on occurrence counts.
explanation: UNION, INTERSECT, and EXCEPT return distinct tuples. Their ALL variants preserve or calculate multiplicities.

INTERSECT ALL emits min(left count,right count) copies; EXCEPT ALL emits max(0,left count minus right count). DISTINCT INTERSECT resembles a semi-join and DISTINCT EXCEPT resembles an anti-join only after duplicates are removed.

without ALL: clamp result multiplicity to 0 or 1
invariants: Distinct variants emit each result tuple at most once.
Bag intersection never emits more copies than either input contains.
Bag difference never yields a negative multiplicity.
pitfalls: Calling concatenation UNION rather than UNION ALL.
Using membership only for an ALL variant.
Treating EXCEPT as symmetric.

labs.title: External Sort and K-Way Merge
labs.subtitle: Sort data larger than memory by forming disk runs, merging their heads, and accounting for every byte and I/O pass.
assignment_brief: Sort num_values unsigned 64-bit little-endian integers from an input File into an output File in ascending order. The data may be much larger than memory.

concepts.title: Phase 1: form sorted runs
concepts.takeaway: Convert one unsorted stream into several independently sorted disk runs, each created from a memory-resident chunk.
explanation: The implementation computes values_that_fit = floor(mem_size / 8). It repeatedly reads at most that many values, sorts the vector with std::sort, writes it to a resized temporary File, and records the file plus its value count as a Run.

The final partial chunk is handled with min(values_per_run, remaining). Each produced run is sorted, covers a disjoint input slice, and preserves every value including duplicates. This implementation uses simple memory-sized quicksort runs; it does not implement the lecture's replacement-selection optimization that can create average runs near twice the memory size.
pseudocode: run := new temporary file sized count * 8
invariants: Every completed run is internally nondecreasing.
The concatenation of run multisets equals the consumed input multiset.
The last run may contain fewer than values_per_run values.
File offsets and lengths are converted from values to bytes exactly once at the I/O boundary.
pitfalls: Treating mem_size bytes as a count of uint64_t values.
Dropping or over-reading the final partial chunk.
Claiming that a value vector of size mem_size alone satisfies the heap limit; run descriptors and File allocations coexist with it.
Forgetting that this simple run-generation strategy can create many more runs than replacement selection.

concepts.title: Phase 2: merge the run frontier
concepts.takeaway: Keep one current candidate per active run; the smallest candidate is the next global output.
explanation: Each RunCursor refills a small sequential input buffer and returns values in its run's sorted order. The min-heap stores {value, run_index}; run_index identifies which cursor to advance after the minimum is emitted.

At every iteration the heap contains the smallest not-yet-emitted value from each nonempty run. Because each run is sorted, no hidden value in a run can be smaller than its head. Popping the global minimum, appending it to the output buffer, and replacing it with the next value from the same run preserves a sorted output frontier.
pseudocode: cursor[i] := buffered cursor over run i
invariants: The heap contains at most one entry per active input run.
Each heap entry is the smallest unconsumed value of its run.
The emitted sequence is nondecreasing.
Every pop advances exactly the run that supplied that value, so values are neither lost nor duplicated.
pitfalls: Using std::priority_queue's default max-heap ordering.
Advancing every run after a pop instead of only the source run.
Dropping equal values; sorting here preserves bag multiplicity.
Reading one uint64_t per system call instead of buffering each run.

concepts.title: The hard memory contract
concepts.takeaway: A memory budget is a sum over all simultaneously live heap allocations, not the largest vector considered in isolation.
explanation: The submitted merge divides values_that_fit between input payload buffers and one output payload buffer. Those payloads alone consume approximately mem_size. It then allocates, outside that accounting, a vector of RunCursor objects, one allocation per cursor buffer, the priority_queue's HeapEntry vector, Run vectors, and heap-allocated PosixFile objects.

On the audited 64-bit ABI, RunCursor is 64 bytes, HeapEntry is 16 bytes, and Run is 16 bytes. With mem_size = 1024, V = 128 values and k = V/4 = 32, input/output payloads request 1024 bytes, cursors request 2048, heap entries need at least 512, the run vector needs at least 512, and 32 File objects add more. An independent global-operator-new counter measured 4,888 additional requested heap bytes—4.77 times the promised 1,024 bytes, excluding allocator metadata.

Run formation and final copy also allocate a value buffer of exactly mem_size while Run/File bookkeeping remains live. Therefore the implementation violates the README's hard ceiling even under a generous interpretation that ignores allocator headers.
pseudocode: reserve fixed metadata and allocator safety margin first
use one preallocated arena or explicitly budget every container capacity
invariants: Peak simultaneous requested heap memory must never exceed mem_size.
Heap capacity, not merely heap size, belongs in the budget.
All k input buffers and the output buffer coexist during a merge.
Run descriptors, cursor arrays, File objects, and vector allocations coexist with payload buffers.
pitfalls: Budgeting only uint64_t payloads and ignoring container/metadata storage.
Using max_runs_per_merge = values_that_fit / 4 without deriving the actual byte cost per run.
Forcing every buffer to at least one value when mem_size cannot hold k inputs plus output.
Treating the optional LimitedMemory test as proof of compliance: it is excluded unless RUN_LIMITED_MEMORY_TEST is defined and permits roughly 2x mem_size plus output storage.
Ignoring transient vector reallocation peaks and allocator bookkeeping.

source_refs.note: Uses mandatory language: no more heap bytes than mem_size.

concepts.title: Fan-in, merge levels, and I/O cost
concepts.takeaway: Larger fan-in reduces merge levels, but only if every run gets enough input buffering and the complete memory budget still holds.
explanation: A balanced external merge sort with R initial runs and feasible fan-in k needs about ceil(log_k R) merge levels. Each full level reads and writes the data once, so run formation plus merge levels dominate I/O. The exact answer must state whether the final output write is counted as a merge write and whether pages or values are the unit.

This implementation caps run count by merging as soon as runs.size() reaches k. That bounds open temporary files, but it collapses the whole current set to one run and later repeatedly merges the ever-growing accumulated run with k-1 fresh runs. The result remains sorted, yet old data is rewritten in many batches instead of balanced levels. For k = 2 it degenerates into merging the accumulated prefix with every new run, yielding quadratic rewrite work in the number of runs.
pseudocode: balanced plan: merge disjoint groups of <= k runs per level
avoid: merge the entire accumulated result after every k-1 new runs
invariants: Every merge input is already sorted.
A merge pass partitions the current run set into disjoint groups.
Each input run is consumed exactly once within a balanced pass.
Fan-in must be derived from memory and useful I/O block sizes, not only the count of uint64_t payload slots.
pitfalls: Counting comparisons but ignoring full-data read/write passes.
Choosing enormous k that leaves one-value input buffers and causes tiny I/O.
Assuming 'bounded number of temporary files' also implies near-optimal I/O.
Forgetting the partial final group in a merge pass.

concepts.title: Block I/O and boundary behavior
concepts.takeaway: The algorithm should turn sorted computation into large sequential reads and writes while preserving the File contract.
explanation: read_values and write_values keep algorithmic positions in values but multiply by 8 when calling the byte-addressed File API. Every temporary and final output file is resized before write, satisfying the test File's strict bounds checks.

RunCursor amortizes read calls by refilling an input vector; output_buffer similarly batches writes. The command-line tool can generate descending or random binary inputs, print them, and invoke the sorter. The benchmark sorts 20,000 random values with an 8 KiB advertised memory size.

For nonempty input and mem_size < 8, the implementation silently truncates output to zero. That is not a valid sorted result and is not specified by the assignment; a production-quality API should reject an impossible budget or define a correct minimal-memory path.
pseudocode: read/write sequential blocks, not one value per syscall
invariants: The output size is num_values * 8 for every successful nonempty sort.
No File write extends beyond the size established by resize.
Only the first num_values input integers are part of the requested sort.
The final output multiset equals the requested input multiset.
pitfalls: Returning an empty output for an impossible memory budget.
Overflowing value_offset * 8, count * 8, or total_values * 8; the implementation has no checked arithmetic.
Trusting native uint64_t reinterpretation on a big-endian host even though the public format is little-endian.
Passing num_values larger than the actual input file.

drills.prompt: Write the k-way merge pseudocode and prove that the next heap minimum is globally safe to emit.
drills.answer: Initialize one current head from every nonempty sorted run. The heap minimum is no larger than every other run head; every unseen value is no smaller than its own run head, so no unseen value can precede the minimum. Emit it, advance only that source run, and insert its new head. Repeat until the heap is empty.
checklist: One frontier value per active run.
Min-heap rather than max-heap.
Advance only the source run.
State the sorted-run invariant.
Flush output without changing logical order.

drills.prompt: Given N pages, B buffer pages, initial runs of B pages, and fan-in B-1, calculate run count, merge levels, and total page I/O.
drills.answer: Initial runs R = ceil(N/B). Merge levels L = ceil(log base (B-1) of R), adjusted for partial groups. Run formation reads and writes N pages. Every complete merge level also reads and writes N pages, so a conventional count is 2N(1+L), unless the final merge streams directly to a consumer or the question uses a different output convention.

Feasible fan-in from buffers.

drills.answer: It does not. The input and output uint64_t buffers already total about mem_size. The measured 1 KiB case requested 4,888 extra heap bytes.

drills.prompt: Why can periodic early merging pass correctness tests but still be a poor external-sort schedule?
drills.answer: Every merge combines sorted runs correctly, so final ordering is preserved. But after each threshold the implementation collapses all current runs, then later merges that increasingly large accumulated run with fresh ones. Old values are repeatedly read and written. Balanced disjoint groups per level rewrite each value only once per level and have logarithmic depth.

Identify the growing accumulated run.
Describe balanced disjoint passes.
Mention the k=2 quadratic degeneration.

drills.prompt: Compare simple memory-sized run formation with replacement selection.
drills.answer: Simple formation fills memory, sorts, writes, and produces runs no longer than memory. Replacement selection maintains eligible and deferred heaps: it emits the smallest eligible value and admits new inputs that do not violate the current run order, often producing average runs about twice memory and one long run for sorted input. It reduces later merge work but adds heap and variable-record memory complexity.

Complexity trade-off.

The submitted code computes values_that_fit = 0, resizes output to zero, and returns, which violates the required result.

The implementation supports only fixed-width uint64_t values and simple quicksort run generation; variable-length tuples, replacement selection, loser trees, direct final streaming, and asynchronous I/O are outside its scope.

labs.title: Expression Interpretation and LLVM Compilation
labs.subtitle: Evaluate one typed expression tree two ways: recursively in C++ and as optimized native code generated through LLVM.
assignment_brief: Implement constants, indexed arguments, explicit casts, and binary arithmetic over signed 64-bit integers and doubles.
Every expression supports two execution paths. evaluate recursively interprets the tree and returns an opaque 64-bit payload; build recursively emits typed LLVM IR for the same semantics.

ExpressionCompiler wraps the generated tree in a function with the raw ABI data64_t compiled_expression(data64_t* args), hands the module to the LLVM ORC JIT, resolves the machine-code address, and executes it.
learning_outcomes: Trace one expression tree through both recursive interpretation and recursive LLVM construction.
Explain why data64_t is a transport container for bits rather than the semantic numeric type.
Distinguish a representation-preserving bitcast from a value-changing numeric cast.
Select typed LLVM instructions for integer and floating arithmetic, including signed integer division.
Reconstruct a formula from SSA definitions and constant-fold it when inputs become compile-time constants.
State the generated function ABI and the lifetime requirements of its module, JIT, context, arguments, and function pointer.
Interpret the benchmark as steady-state execution cost only, and identify the operations and edge cases it does not measure.

concepts.title: One tree, two execution strategies
concepts.takeaway: The interpreter computes now; the compiler constructs a typed program that computes later.
explanation: evaluate walks the expression tree at runtime. A binary node recursively evaluates its children, decodes their raw payloads according to the node's ValueType, performs the C++ operation, and re-encodes the result.

build performs the same structural recursion but returns llvm::Value objects. It emits IR nodes such as add or fadd instead of calculating the answer. ExpressionCompiler supplies the function and entry block around the recursively generated body.

recursively build typed child llvm::Value objects
invariants: Both children of a binary node have the same semantic ValueType.
Interpreter and compiled paths implement the same value semantics for defined inputs.
The expression objects must outlive interpretation or compilation because parents store child references.
pitfalls: Computing a value inside build instead of emitting IR.
Choosing an integer LLVM instruction for a DOUBLE node or an FP instruction for INT64.

concepts.title: Opaque data64_t transport and the generated ABI
concepts.takeaway: Every argument and result crosses the C++/JIT boundary as exactly 64 raw bits; ValueType tells the code how to interpret those bits.
explanation: data64_t is uint64_t because signed integers and IEEE doubles are both eight bytes. An integer payload contains the two's-complement bits of int64_t; a double payload contains the double's IEEE representation.

The generated function has the ABI i64 compiled_expression(ptr args). INT64 Argument nodes load i64. DOUBLE Argument nodes load double from the corresponding eight-byte slot. A DOUBLE root is bitcast to i64 before return so the external function signature remains uniform.

DOUBLE argument: load double from the same eight-byte slot[index]
DOUBLE result: bitcast double -> i64 for transport
caller decodes returned bits using root ValueType

The caller encodes each slot according to the Argument node's declared ValueType.
A DOUBLE result is representation-bitcast, not numerically converted, at the ABI boundary.

concepts.title: Numeric conversion is not bit reinterpretation
concepts.takeaway: Cast changes the numeric value's representation; bitcast merely preserves the same bits under another type.
explanation: The assignment highlights that integer 42 and double 42.0 have different bit patterns. A semantic cast must decode the source, numerically convert it, and encode the target.

The interpreter uses static_cast after std::bit_cast decoding. The compiler uses signed-integer-to-floating SIToFP and floating-to-signed-integer FPToSI. By contrast, the final DOUBLE result uses a bitcast only because it is being packed into the raw return ABI without changing its value.

drills.prompt: Read a supplied straight-line LLVM function, rewrite its SSA definitions as one arithmetic expression, substitute known globals, and constant-fold the result.
drills.answer: Start at ret and recursively substitute each SSA definition. Respect opcode types and signedness. Replace compile-time-known globals, evaluate constant arithmetic and comparisons, select the surviving branch, then remove dead definitions and unreachable blocks.
checklist: Follow SSA use-def chains from the return value.
Track each value's LLVM type.
Distinguish sdiv/udiv and signed/unsigned comparisons.
Substitute only values explicitly known at compile time.
Remove dead code only after proving it cannot affect the result.

drills.prompt: Explain why casting integer 42 to DOUBLE must not use a bitcast.
drills.answer: The raw bits for integer 42 represent a tiny unrelated double. Numeric cast SIToFP computes double 42.0 with its own IEEE bit pattern; bitcast is appropriate only when packing or unpacking an already-computed value across the raw data64_t ABI.
checklist: Name the two distinct bit patterns.
Use SIToFP for signed INT64 to DOUBLE.
Use FPToSI for DOUBLE to signed INT64.
Reserve bitcast for representation transport.

drills.prompt: Debug an implementation that emits udiv for every INT64 division.
drills.answer: The expression type is signed INT64 even though data64_t is uint64_t. Decode/interpret the payload as signed and emit sdiv. A direct case such as -7/2 should produce -3 with truncation toward zero.
checklist: Do not infer semantic signedness from the transport type.
Use a negative direct test.
Mention division-by-zero and INT64_MIN/-1.
Keep interpreter and compiled policies aligned.

drills.prompt: Sketch the LLVM wrapper function for a DOUBLE root and explain every conversion.
drills.answer: Declare i64 @compiled_expression(ptr args), recursively build a typed double result, bitcast that double to i64 without changing bits, and ret i64. Typed child Cast nodes still use numeric conversion instructions.
checklist: Use a uniform raw external ABI.
Load each Argument using its semantic type.
Bitcast only the final DOUBLE result for transport.
Keep the JIT alive while calling the resolved address.

drills.prompt: What conclusion can and cannot be drawn from the provided interpreter-versus-compiled benchmark?
drills.answer: It compares steady-state calls for one 1,000-node left-deep INT64 Add/Sub/Mul tree after JIT compilation. It can show virtual tree-walk overhead versus optimized straight-line code, but excludes compilation cost and does not cover casts, division, doubles, branches, changing inputs, or end-to-end queries.
checklist: State that compile time is outside the timed loop.
Name the exact operations and tree shape.
Note that inputs are fixed during timing.
Flag signed-overflow undefined behavior in the interpreted workload.

limitations: The project has no accompanying student report; all conclusions come from README, code, tests, benchmark, JIT wrapper, examples, and lecture evidence.
The current host lacks cmake and an LLVM 21 development installation, so the 29 provided tests and benchmark were not executed in this audit.
Constant constructors and many tests decode/encode via reinterpret_cast lvalue dereferences; std::bit_cast or memcpy is safer under C++ aliasing rules.
Interpreter INT64 add/sub/mul use signed C++ arithmetic, where overflow is undefined, while plain LLVM integer arithmetic wraps modulo 2^64; equivalence is not defined on overflow.
Integer division by zero and INT64_MIN/-1 are unguarded; DOUBLE-to-INT64 conversion of NaN, infinity, or out-of-range values is also undefined/poison territory.
Argument lookup has no runtime argument count, bounds check, type tag, NULL flag, or alignment check.
Expression nodes hold child references rather than ownership, so child lifetimes must exceed parent evaluation or compilation.
ExpressionCompiler is effectively one-shot, does not guard run-before-compile, and does not reject a null symbol pointer.
JIT::addModule prints invalid-module diagnostics but still forwards the module to the optimization/compile layer.
The benchmark excludes compilation cost, covers only INT64 Add/Sub/Mul in a left-deep tree, uses fixed inputs, and likely invokes signed-overflow undefined behavior in the interpreter.
